paragraphs: Scaling laws help researchers predict how a larger model will perform using results from smaller, cheaper training runs. Their usefulness depends on how those relationships are estimated. This paper examines that estimation process using a released collection of losses and downstream evaluations from 485 previously published pretrained models, fitting more than 1,000 scaling laws.

One finding is that measurements taken during training contain valuable information: including intermediate checkpoints substantially improves prediction accuracy compared with using final losses alone. Holding other factors equal, predictions are generally most accurate when they come from models near the target model’s size. However, variation between random seeds means that several small training runs can sometimes provide more useful evidence than one large run.

The authors also find that differences between model families need not prevent useful transfer. A single model with the target architecture, combined with scaling parameters estimated from other families, can often predict the target’s behavior. Together, these findings guide how to allocate training experiments and extract more information from their results.
icml-2025-a-hitchhikers-guide-to-scaling.tldr: A large study of scaling-law estimation identifies practical ways to improve predictions using intermediate checkpoints, nearby model sizes, repeated runs, and information from other model families.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to choose which vertices of a graph should have their labels revealed. The objective is to select k vertices whose labels will be most useful for predicting labels elsewhere in the graph. The setting is offline: the problem centers on selecting a set of vertices, under a theoretical model motivated by smoothness of labels across the graph.

Previously, algorithms with theoretical guarantees in this model were available only for restricted graph families, including trees. The authors extend the algorithmic picture to general weighted graphs. Their result uses O(log n) resource augmentation, meaning the guarantee allows an enlargement of the selection resource that scales logarithmically with graph size. That qualification is central to understanding what the algorithm achieves.

The paper also establishes constant hardness of approximation, identifying an obstacle to obtaining arbitrarily accurate approximation guarantees. The algorithm and hardness result together clarify the computational landscape: useful guarantees extend beyond simple graph structures, while approximation remains constrained by intrinsic difficulty.
icml-2025-algorithms-and-hardness-for-ac.tldr: The paper gives a resource-augmented active-learning algorithm for general weighted graphs and establishes a complementary approximation-hardness result.

paragraphs: When some classes have far more examples than others, learning a useful classifier becomes especially challenging. This paper develops a theoretical framework for that problem in both binary and multiclass settings. It questions the foundations of common remedies and demonstrates a failure of Bayes consistency for cost-sensitive methods: their objectives need not lead to the ideal classification rule considered by the analysis.

The proposed alternative is a margin loss designed for class imbalance. Margins describe how confidently a classifier separates competing decisions. The authors prove strong H-consistency for their loss, connecting optimization of that loss to classification performance within a hypothesis class. They also derive learning guarantees using empirical loss and a class-sensitive version of Rademacher complexity, which captures aspects of the model class relevant to generalization.

These results motivate IMMAX, a family of algorithms that incorporate confidence margins and support different hypothesis sets. Although theory is the main contribution, the paper also reports extensive experiments showing effectiveness against existing baselines. The framework connects the training objective, generalization analysis, and practical algorithm design.
icml-2025-balancing-the-scales-a-theoret.tldr: IMMAX combines an imbalance-aware margin loss with consistency and generalization guarantees to support learning from uneven class distributions.

paragraphs: Beyond The Rainbow builds on the idea that several complementary improvements can jointly make a reinforcement-learning agent much stronger. Starting from Rainbow DQN, the authors integrate six additional improvements drawn from the reinforcement-learning literature. Their aim includes both strong game-playing performance and computational efficiency on a high-end desktop computer.

On Atari-60, the resulting BTR algorithm achieves a human-normalized interquartile mean score of 7.6, which the authors report as a new state of the art for reinforcement learning using a desktop PC. They also report training on 200 million Atari frames within 12 hours. These results place performance and training cost together, making the available computing setup part of the contribution.

The evaluation extends to Super Mario Galaxy, Mario Kart, and Mortal Kombat, where agents are successfully trained with minimal algorithmic changes. This provides evidence that BTR’s usefulness extends beyond Atari. Detailed component ablations examine the contributions of individual improvements using multiple measures, helping assess how the combined system achieves its results.
icml-2025-beyond-the-rainbow-high-perfor.tldr: BTR combines six improvements to Rainbow DQN to achieve strong game-playing results with training feasible on a high-end desktop PC.

paragraphs: Cardinality sketches estimate the number of distinct elements while keeping only a compact summary of the data. Their small size reduces storage, communication, and computation. However, queries chosen adaptively can undermine their reliability: earlier research showed breakdown after roughly a quadratic number of queries in the sketch size k, up to logarithmic factors.

This paper designs robust estimators whose guarantees depend on how often individual elements recur across queries. The constructions can support exponentially many adaptive queries, provided each element appears in at most roughly k squared queries, again up to logarithmic factors. The key condition therefore concerns repeated participation by the same element, rather than the overall query count.

This distinction matters when a large collection of queries spreads its attention across many different elements. In that case, total query volume can be much larger than the participation count for any single element. The result moves the quadratic restriction to this finer measure of overlap, giving a more flexible robustness guarantee without claiming unrestricted resistance to every adaptive query sequence.
icml-2025-breaking-the-quadratic-barrier.tldr: New cardinality estimators support exponentially many adaptive queries when each element participates in only a bounded, roughly quadratic number of queries.

paragraphs: The paper studies agents estimating a shared vector of means from normal distributions when sampling costs differ across agents and coordinates. Sharing data can help each agent obtain expensive information in exchange for samples it can collect cheaply. The difficulty is organizing this exchange so that participation is worthwhile and strategic actions, including fabricated data or failure to collect samples, do not undermine collaboration.

The authors construct a mechanism with an associated Nash equilibrium that is individually rational for all agents. Its social penalty combines estimation errors and collection costs. The mechanism achieves an O(sqrt(m)) approximation to the minimum social penalty in the worst case, and a constant-factor approximation under favorable conditions, where m is the number of agents.

Three hardness results show limits on stronger guarantees involving truthful dominant strategies, individual rationality regardless of others’ actions, and the best available equilibrium’s worst-case social penalty. The paper also incorporates axiomatic bargaining to produce fairer outcomes than minimizing social penalty alone. Thus, efficiency, incentives, and the distribution of benefits all shape the proposed collaboration.
icml-2025-collaborative-mean-estimation-.tldr: A data-sharing mechanism balances estimation costs, strategic incentives, and fairness, with equilibrium guarantees and matching constraints on what stronger mechanisms can achieve.

paragraphs: Causal diagrams compactly represent assumptions about how variables influence one another. This paper develops tools for using those diagrams to reason about counterfactual quantities: questions involving what would happen under alternative circumstances. The central challenge is extracting the relationships and constraints that the underlying causal structure imposes on those quantities.

The authors introduce Ancestral Multi-world Networks, an efficient graphical construction for reading counterfactual independences through d-separation. The construction is sound and complete for this purpose. In plain terms, the graphical procedure correctly identifies the relevant independences implied by the causal diagram and captures all such independences within the stated framework. This gives counterfactual reasoning a structured graphical basis.

The paper also introduces a counterfactual calculus consisting of three transformation rules justified by constraints encoded in the diagram. These rules extend Pearl’s do-calculus from intervention questions to counterfactual reasoning. Together, the network construction and calculus provide complementary tools: one exposes independence relationships, while the other uses diagram-supported constraints to transform quantities of interest.
icml-2025-counterfactual-graphical-model.tldr: Ancestral Multi-world Networks and a three-rule counterfactual calculus extend graphical causal reasoning to counterfactual independences and quantities.

paragraphs: The paper examines how neural networks develop representations that capture information useful for a task. A common distinction separates rich learning, where features adapt to the task, from lazy learning, where the network behaves like a random-feature model. The authors argue that this two-way classification misses important differences arising from learning algorithms, architectures, and data.

Their framework studies the geometry of representations rather than inspecting individual features. It tracks task-relevant manifolds, the geometric structures formed by related representations, as learning proceeds. This perspective asks how entire patterns of representation change, providing a way to distinguish learning processes that might otherwise receive the same broad label.

Theoretical and empirical results show these manifolds becoming untangled as networks learn features. Changes in their geometry reveal different stages and strategies of learning beyond the lazy–rich split. The framework also provides insights into structural inductive biases in neural circuits and mechanisms relevant to out-of-distribution generalization. Its contribution is a more detailed language for analyzing feature learning across artificial networks and neuroscience.
icml-2025-feature-learning-beyond-the-la.tldr: Tracking the geometry of task-relevant representations reveals learning stages and strategies that the lazy–rich distinction misses.

paragraphs: Models that caption images and short clips can struggle to describe long videos coherently because they observe only limited spans of time. This paper addresses the problem by combining descriptions from short segments into a structured representation of the whole video. The aim is to retain both the broad context and details that could be lost during aggregation.

The pipeline first uses existing visual captioning models to describe individual frames or short intervals. It converts those descriptions into scene graphs, then consolidates the graphs into one unified representation. A lightweight graph-to-text decoder produces the final caption from that representation. The graph serves as the intermediate structure connecting local observations with a video-level description.

The framework requires no additional fine-tuning on long-video datasets, extending the usefulness of existing captioning models. Experiments report significantly better results than existing LLM-based consolidation approaches, strong zero-shot performance, and substantially lower computational costs. These findings support structured graph consolidation as an effective way to assemble detailed long-video captions from shorter observations.
icml-2025-fine-grained-captioning-of-lon.tldr: Consolidating short-segment scene graphs produces detailed long-video captions without additional long-video fine-tuning and with lower reported computational costs.

paragraphs: Generating crystal structures requires respecting the geometry and symmetries of crystalline data. Atomic positions expressed as fractional coordinates within a unit cell are periodic, so they live on a hypertorus rather than an ordinary flat coordinate space. This makes their treatment a central challenge for diffusion-based material generation, alongside the multiple kinds of information describing a crystal.

Kinetic Langevin Diffusion for Materials, or KLDM, changes how those coordinates are modeled. It generalizes the Trivialized Diffusion Model to accommodate crystal symmetries and pairs coordinates with auxiliary velocity variables in Euclidean space. This coupling shifts the diffusion process to flat space while enabling effective diffusion over the periodic coordinate domain.

The resulting training objective accounts for the periodic translation symmetry of the underlying data distribution. The authors evaluate KLDM on crystal structure prediction and generation of new structures, reporting performance competitive with current state-of-the-art models. The contribution is a symmetry-aware treatment of coordinates that supports crystal generation while addressing the particular geometry of atomic positions.
icml-2025-kinetic-langevin-diffusion-for.tldr: KLDM couples periodic atomic coordinates with auxiliary velocities to build a symmetry-aware diffusion model with competitive crystal-generation performance.

paragraphs: An LLM-based system benefits from recognizing when an answer may be unreliable. It can then send the question to another expert or choose a safe fallback. This paper studies whether models can communicate confidence in their own correctness well enough for those signals to improve downstream decisions, rather than merely sounding confident.

The proposed method, Self-Reflection with Error-based Feedback, uses a lightweight training strategy to teach this behavior. It introduces confidence tokens into the model and extracts a confidence score from them. These tokens provide a trained signal about answer correctness that can be used when deciding whether to accept an answer, reject it, or route the question elsewhere.

The authors compare confidence tokens with conventional approaches based on verbal confidence statements and token probabilities. They report significant empirical improvements in routing and rejection-learning tasks. The finding concerns the practical usefulness of the confidence signal: in the evaluated settings, the learned tokens support better downstream decisions about which model outputs to rely on.
icml-2025-learning-to-route-llms-with-co.tldr: Self-REF trains LLMs to emit confidence tokens that empirically improve decisions about routing questions and rejecting unreliable answers.

paragraphs: The static Schrödinger bridge problem seeks the most likely stochastic evolution connecting two prescribed probability distributions. A standard solution strategy moves to a dual formulation and applies Sinkhorn’s algorithm to find optimal potential functions. For the classical problem, this iterative procedure is known to converge linearly under mild assumptions.

This paper extends that foundation to a generalized bridge problem allowing any strictly increasing divergence functional, substantially broadening the role played by the usual entropy expression. Such generalized problems arise across entropic optimal transport, random graphs and matrices, and combinatorics. The question is whether the dual formulation and convergence guarantees survive this broader choice of functional.

The authors establish Kantorovich duality and linear convergence of Sinkhorn’s algorithm for the generalized problem under mild conditions. Linear convergence describes geometric reduction of the relevant error as iterations proceed. These results give a rigorous basis for Sinkhorn-type methods across a wider family of bridge problems, with the stated conditions remaining part of the guarantee.
icml-2025-linear-convergence-of-sinkhorn.tldr: The paper establishes duality and conditional linear convergence for Sinkhorn’s algorithm across a broad generalization of the static Schrödinger bridge problem.

paragraphs: Claims that foundation models are approaching a shared representation space depend on how similarity between models is measured. Usually, that measurement uses representations of examples from a particular dataset. This paper asks whether the apparent relationships between models remain consistent when the examples used for comparison change.

The authors propose a systematic framework for measuring this variation across stimulus sets. They find that the training objective strongly influences consistency. In particular, self-supervised vision models show relative pairwise similarities that transfer better across datasets than those of image-classification or image-text models. The finding concerns stability of relationships between representations across datasets, rather than simply how similar two models look on one collection of examples.

The connection between representational similarity and task behavior also depends on the dataset, appearing most strongly for single-domain datasets. These results make the choice of evaluation stimuli part of the interpretation of representation comparisons. The framework helps assess whether an observed similarity pattern generalizes across datasets and how it relates to differences in model behavior.
icml-2025-objective-drives-the-consisten.tldr: Training objectives influence how consistently model-representation similarities transfer across datasets, and their relationship to task behavior is also dataset-dependent.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between spaces of functions. Deep Operator Networks and Fourier Neural Operators already have universal approximation guarantees, but representational capability alone does not establish that gradient descent will successfully train them. This paper addresses that optimization question through a unified framework applicable to both architectures.

The authors show that the losses for these neural operators satisfy restricted strong convexity and smoothness, two properties that guarantee loss decreases under gradient descent. Although the same framework covers both models, the architectural reasons supporting these properties differ. This makes the analysis sensitive to how the networks are constructed while still yielding a shared route to convergence guarantees.

A central consequence is that increasing network width benefits the optimization guarantees for both model families. Experiments on canonical operator-learning problems support the theory, with larger widths improving training. The result connects an architectural choice to the behavior of the training algorithm, complementing existing guarantees about which functions these networks can represent.
icml-2025-optimization-for-neural-operat.tldr: A unified analysis gives gradient-descent convergence guarantees for two neural-operator families and shows how greater width can benefit training.

paragraphs: Hypergradient descent adjusts a learning rate during optimization, but the method long lacked a rigorous convergence analysis. This paper supplies such an analysis using an online-learning framework. The authors use the resulting understanding to develop adaptive gradient methods with both theoretical support and empirical evidence.

The analysis shows that hypergradient descent automatically identifies the optimal step size for the local optimization landscape and achieves local superlinear convergence. The local qualification matters: the result describes behavior near the relevant solution region. The theory also explains previously reported instability and motivates efficient strategies for addressing it. Two additional variants incorporate heavy-ball and Nesterov momentum.

Experiments on deterministic convex problems find that the heavy-ball variant, HDM-HB, performs robustly and significantly outperforms other adaptive first-order methods. It also often matches L-BFGS while requiring less memory and cheaper iterations. Together, these results connect an established learning-rate heuristic to a rigorous analysis and show practical benefits in the tested optimization setting.
icml-2025-provable-and-practical-online-.tldr: An online-learning analysis explains hypergradient descent’s convergence and instability, supporting momentum variants with strong results on deterministic convex problems.

paragraphs: Forecasts for related time series can benefit from information shared across sequences. Existing relational models exploit such connections to predict values, but uncertainty estimation has received less attention. This paper asks how relationships between sequences can also help construct prediction intervals, which express a range of possible future values.

Conformal Relational Prediction, or CoRel, combines conformal prediction, quantile regression, and graph deep-learning operators. Its interval construction uses relationships among time series rather than treating every target sequence independently. The method does not require a graph of those relationships to be supplied beforehand and can operate on top of any pretrained predictor.

CoRel also includes an adaptive component for non-exchangeable data and changes in the input sequences. This addresses the sequential setting in which observations need not behave as interchangeable samples. The authors report accurate coverage and state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification on relevant benchmarks. The contribution extends relational information from improving point forecasts to improving how uncertainty around those forecasts is represented.
icml-2025-relational-conformal-predictio.tldr: CoRel uses relationships among time series to construct adaptive prediction intervals on top of pretrained forecasting models.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of edge transition probabilities on a binary tree from repeated observations at its leaves. A character evolves along the edges according to a two-state symmetric Markov process. This models a branch-length estimation problem in phylogenetics and relates to inference in latent tree graphical models.

Although the likelihood can be non-concave and contain many critical points, coordinate maximization has worked well in practice. The authors provide a conditional theoretical explanation. For a balanced tree, deep within the Kesten–Stigum reconstruction regime and with polynomially many samples, they identify a parameter region independent of tree size where the log-likelihood is strongly concave and smooth with high probability.

On that favorable likelihood event, coordinate maximization converges exponentially fast to the maximum likelihood estimator when initialized sufficiently close. With m samples, that estimator lies within O(1/sqrt(m)) of the true parameter. The result links sample availability, local landscape geometry, and initialization to reliable estimation, explaining success within the specified regime despite the general likelihood’s complexity.
icml-2025-sample-complexity-of-branch-le.tldr: Under specified tree, sampling, parameter, and initialization conditions, coordinate maximization rapidly recovers an accurate maximum likelihood branch-length estimate.

paragraphs: SelfCite aims to improve the sentence-level citations that LLMs attach to generated answers. Producing suitable training annotations can be costly, so the method obtains a reward signal from the model itself. It evaluates citations by changing the context available to the model and observing whether the response remains supported by that context.

The procedure tests two complementary properties. For necessity, it removes the cited text: a necessary citation should contain information whose removal prevents the same response. For sufficiency, it keeps only the cited text: sufficient evidence should preserve the response. These context-ablation tests turn the relationship between an answer and its cited passages into a self-supervised signal.

The reward can rank candidate outputs during best-of-N sampling or guide preference optimization to fine-tune a model for better citations. Across five long-form question-answering tasks in LongBench-Cite, the authors report citation F1 improvements of up to 5.3 points. The approach thus supports both inference-time selection and training-time improvement using the same underlying attribution test.
icml-2025-selfcite-self-supervised-align.tldr: SelfCite uses context-removal and context-retention tests to reward better sentence-level citations, improving citation F1 by up to 5.3 points.

paragraphs: This study compares supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning as ways to improve foundation models after pretraining. It focuses on whether learned behavior transfers to unfamiliar textual rules and visual variations. The authors introduce the arithmetic card game GeneralPoints and use the V-IRL navigation environment to examine these forms of generalization.

In the studied settings, reinforcement learning generalizes across textual rule changes and visual variants, particularly when training uses an outcome-based reward. Supervised fine-tuning instead tends to memorize training data and struggles on out-of-distribution variants. Further analysis attributes part of RL’s visual generalization gains to improvements in the model’s underlying visual recognition capabilities.

The results also identify a complementary role for supervised fine-tuning. It stabilizes the model’s output format, which the study finds essential for effective subsequent RL training and its performance gains. The findings therefore support a sequence in which SFT establishes usable response behavior and RL develops more transferable capabilities. The reported contrast concerns the evaluated multimodal tasks and variants.
icml-2025-sft-memorizes-rl-generalizes-a.tldr: In the studied multimodal tasks, RL generalizes better to unseen variants, while SFT supplies the stable output format needed for effective RL training.

paragraphs: The Local Glivenko–Cantelli setting studies how uniformly the empirical mean approaches its target, with convergence rates that depend on the underlying distribution. This paper asks whether restricting attention to that familiar estimator leaves room for major improvements. It broadens the setting to allow arbitrary estimators and examines what this additional freedom can achieve.

Two questions organize the analysis: can another estimator learn a strictly larger collection of probability measures, and can it make risk decrease faster? The authors give negative answers to both when the learner is prohibited from exploiting certain infinite-dimensional pathologies. Under that restriction, the empirical mean is minimax optimal, so the broader choice of estimators does not improve those fundamental learning possibilities.

The restriction is consequential. When the exceptional infinite-dimensional constructions are allowed, a strictly larger class of measures becomes learnable. The paper therefore establishes both an optimality result and a boundary to that result. Its conclusion depends on which mathematical behaviors are permitted, clarifying why an unrestricted statement of empirical-mean optimality would be too strong.
icml-2025-the-empirical-mean-is-minimax-.tldr: The empirical mean is minimax optimal in the Local Glivenko–Cantelli setting when certain infinite-dimensional exploits are excluded.

paragraphs: Unequal access to LLM tools can give applicants different opportunities to improve their resumes, affecting both hiring accuracy and fairness. This paper models that problem through a variant of strategic classification that accommodates different degrees of manipulation and stochastic outcomes. The framework explicitly treats LLM-assisted changes as part of the hiring process.

The proposed two-ticket scheme applies another manipulation to each submitted resume and evaluates that version alongside the submission. The authors prove fairness and accuracy improvements when the hiring objective maximizes the true positive rate subject to a no-false-positives constraint. That objective and constraint are part of the theoretical result, rather than a guarantee for every possible screening policy.

The analysis extends to an n-ticket scheme, where hiring outcomes converge to a fixed, group-independent decision, eliminating disparities due to differential LLM access within the framework. Experiments using real resumes and an open-source screening tool support the two-ticket approach. The central idea is to incorporate additional transformations into evaluation so that applicants’ unequal manipulation opportunities have less influence on decisions.
icml-2025-two-tickets-are-better-than-on.tldr: Evaluating submitted resumes alongside additional LLM-manipulated versions improves fairness and accuracy under the paper’s constrained hiring objective.

paragraphs: Video language models commonly rely on visual encoders from a single backbone family, which limits the range of visual information they can process. MERV, the Multi-Encoder Video Representation, brings several encoders together so their different capabilities can contribute to a more comprehensive representation. The challenge is combining heterogeneous features efficiently and coherently.

MERV first aligns encoder outputs across space and time. It then projects them into a shared structure and combines them using cross-attention. This sequence makes features from different encoders compatible before fusion, allowing the model to draw on multiple sources of visual information within one video representation.

Under fair comparison, the authors report accuracy up to 4.62% higher than the base model with few extra parameters. After visual processing is parallelized, training is also faster than equivalent single-encoder methods. Qualitative analysis indicates that MERV captures and combines domain knowledge from its individual encoders. These findings support integrating specialized visual representations as a route toward stronger video understanding.
icml-2025-unifying-specialized-visual-en.tldr: MERV aligns and fuses multiple visual encoders, improving reported video-model accuracy with few additional parameters and faster training after parallelization.

paragraphs: Vector graphics describe images through shapes, but their discrete and complex structure makes generative modeling challenging. GRIMOIRE generates SVG graphics from text while learning shapes from raster images. This supervision choice allows shape learning to draw on image data without requiring corresponding SVG examples.

The model contains two modules. A Visual Shape Quantizer reconstructs raster images as vector shapes and maps them into a discrete codebook. An autoregressive transformer then models the joint distribution of shape tokens, their positions, and textual descriptions. Together, these modules connect learned visual shape components with language-guided generation of complete vector graphics.

The authors demonstrate closed, filled shapes on MNIST and Emoji data, and outline strokes on icon and font data. They report higher generative quality than previous image-supervised methods and greater flexibility than a vector-supervised approach. The contribution is a route from raster supervision to reusable vector shape tokens, followed by a model that arranges those tokens in response to natural-language descriptions.
icml-2025-vector-grimoire-codebook-based.tldr: GRIMOIRE learns vector shape tokens from raster images and uses a text-conditioned transformer to generate SVG graphics.

paragraphs: A time series can have several plausible futures, so forecasting benefits from representing alternatives. TimeMCL adapts Multiple Choice Learning to this task. It uses a neural network with several prediction heads, allowing one model to produce multiple candidate futures for multivariate time series.

Training uses a Winner-Takes-All loss to encourage diversity among the predictions. The authors connect this behavior to an implicit quantization objective: the collection of predictions represents different possible futures through a finite set of alternatives. This perspective helps explain why a multiple-head system can address ambiguity while retaining a relatively simple learning setup.

The paper uses synthetic data to investigate the approach and evaluates it on real-world time series. The reported results show promising forecasting performance at a light computational cost. The contribution is both methodological and explanatory: it adapts Multiple Choice Learning to forecasting and relates the diversity of its outputs to the objective the model implicitly pursues. The findings support an efficient approach to producing several plausible forecasts.
icml-2025-winner-takes-all-for-multivari.tldr: TimeMCL uses multiple prediction heads and a Winner-Takes-All loss to forecast diverse plausible futures with light computational cost.

paragraphs: WMAdapter adds user-specified watermark information while a latent diffusion model generates an image. The goal is to support watermarking while preserving image quality. Its plugin design keeps the diffusion components intact, addressing the visual-artifact problem associated with incorporating watermark information into image generation.

The method introduces a contextual adapter that uses the content of the cover image to produce adaptive watermark embeddings. This makes the embedding depend on the image being watermarked. An additional fine-tuning step and a hybrid fine-tuning strategy suppress noticeable artifacts while preserving the integrity of the diffusion components. These mechanisms jointly address how to insert the watermark and how to maintain the visual result.

The authors report strong flexibility, superior image quality, and competitive watermark robustness in their empirical evaluation. They describe the resulting images as sharp and artifact-free. The contribution is a controllable watermarking plugin that combines content-aware embeddings with training strategies aimed at visual quality, while retaining the original diffusion components.
icml-2025-wmadapter-adding-watermark-con.tldr: WMAdapter embeds user-selected watermarks during diffusion generation using content-aware adapters, with strong reported image quality and competitive robustness.
